description: In this explainer we walk operators and serious students through a disciplined approach to learning market demand without falling into the trap of self‑deception. We start by exposing the *illusion of demand* – the tendency to over‑interpret a handful of interviews or surveys as proof of a massive market. We then show how to *translate the customer voice* into a structured hierarchy of needs, emphasizing that the research process (sampling, prompts, coding, aggregation) is an organizational activity that must be transparent (see Griffin & Hauser, 1993 https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.12.1.1). Next, we draw on Kahneman & Tversky’s work on framing and reference points to explain the *reality of choice*: expressed preferences differ from actual purchasing behavior because of framing, switching costs, and procurement rules (Prospect Theory, 1979 https://doi.org/10.2307/1914185). We introduce the *bounded evidence ladder* – a seven‑step checklist (claim, sample, method, raw evidence, counter‑evidence, transfer uncertainty, next reversible test) that forces teams to record what they know and what they don’t (see the report’s ladder description). We then broaden the lens to *reading market and competitors*, highlighting Narver & Slater’s market‑orientation framework that stresses inter‑functional coordination (1990 https://doi.org/10.1177/002224299005400403) and warning against relying on public competitor signals alone. Finally, we list *negative controls* – guardrails such as “interview enthusiasm ≠ purchase commitment” and “one large request ≠ market segment” – and stress the importance of matching evidence scope to industry constraints (e.g., regulated healthcare vs. reversible SaaS decisions). By the end you’ll have a practical, evidence‑producing toolkit to turn customer discovery into a reliable decision‑making system rather than a story‑validation ritual.

title: Customer Discovery & Demand Evidence: Avoiding Illusions and Building an Evidence Ladder
